scoreNote: Strong (5): a recommendation-appropriate response that shows a mandate would punish the families least able to comply and drain volunteering of its value, then offers a better path of encouragement; persuasive.

sentences.text: Schools work better when parents are involved, and few would deny that a child benefits when their family takes an interest in their education.
From this truth the recommendation draws a rule: that all parents should be required to volunteer time at their children's schools.

Parental involvement is valuable and should be encouraged, but requiring it would be unfair, impractical, and self-defeating, because the parents least able to comply are often the ones whose children need the most help.

sections.role: Body — A mandate punishes the struggling

sentences.text: First, a requirement to volunteer would fall hardest on the parents least able to meet it.
A single mother working two jobs, a father on a night shift, or a family caring for a sick relative cannot easily give hours to a school, however much they may wish to.
To require their time is to set up many devoted parents to fail, exposing them to blame for a duty their circumstances make impossible.
And it is exactly these overstretched families whose children most need support, so a mandate would punish the vulnerable and widen the gap between rich and poor schools.
A rule the wealthy can satisfy easily and the struggling cannot is not fairness but a hidden penalty on poverty.
The families with the least time to give are usually the ones whose children most need a school that helps.
Good intentions do not make an impossible demand reasonable.
Moreover, the word required contradicts the very thing that makes volunteering valuable.
Volunteering means giving freely, and an obligation enforced by penalty is no longer volunteering but conscription.
Forced volunteers tend to show up resentful and contribute grudgingly, which helps a school far less than a few willing hands.
The genuine involvement that benefits children grows from interest and goodwill, neither of which can be commanded into being.
A parent dragged to a classroom under threat is unlikely to inspire anyone, including their own child.
A school full of grudging conscripts is no better off than a school with none.
Help offered under threat is rarely much help at all.
Compulsion may produce attendance, but it cannot produce the engagement that actually matters.
However, the recommendation rightly senses that parental involvement matters enormously.
Schools genuinely benefit when parents help, and a culture of involvement is well worth actively building.
But the way to build it is to invite, enable, and welcome parents — flexible hours, meaningful roles, real appreciation — not to threaten them.
Make involvement easy and rewarding and most parents will give what they can; make it a legal duty and you breed only resentment and excuses.
People give most generously when they are asked, not when they are ordered.
Encouragement builds participation; compulsion builds resistance.
In conclusion, parents should be strongly encouraged to help their children's schools, but not required to.
A mandate would burden the families least able to bear it and drain volunteering of the goodwill that gives it value, achieving less than a warm invitation would.
The goal is willing partners in a child's education, and willingness is precisely what a requirement destroys.
